purpose: Lossless call wrapper for source-bound reuse; no new review occurred.

questions.question: What evidence do the three papers supply?
questions.answer: The opening distinguishes mathematical memory models, paired macaque neural and eye recordings, and spatial activity in rodents and bats. These settings and questions match the three primary abstracts.

questions.question: Does grouping them imply one observed biological circuit?
questions.answer: No. The settings are distinct and the place overview leaves combining them in one circuit as a research question.

questions.question: Why do variable signals matter for these behaviors?
questions.answer: Remembering a direction, maintaining gaze and tracking location need usable representations despite brief variable neural signals. Models connect cell assumptions to predictions; recordings test those predictions.

questions.question: Does “hold an angle” claim the eye is motionless?
questions.answer: No. It states the task goal; the next eye overview explicitly describes drift during fixation.

questions.question: Does persistent activity ensure an accurate value?
questions.answer: The passage distinguishes continuing activity from a changing value. Its small-fluctuation calculation and information lower bound agree with Burak and Fiete pp. 1–2 and the inspected information chapter. Reading longer has diminishing benefit because the value changes.

questions.question: Does high information guarantee stable memory?
questions.answer: No. The text calls the result a lower bound; the earlier information chapter explicitly says high information allows small diffusion but does not guarantee it.

questions.question: What does the 82 percent result establish?
questions.answer: It estimates common upstream horizontal displacement variance over 350 ms from 57 OMNs in two macaques. Calibration, prediction and separate circuit modeling are distinguished. Main pp. 2–5 and Eqs. 11–17 support the number and its interpretation.

questions.question: Does 82 percent mean path length or a direct integrator recording?
questions.answer: No. The text says displacement variance and explicitly states that the memory circuit is not uniquely located. The source note also rejects direct integrator recording.

questions.question: Does the spatial model measure random wiring?
questions.answer: No. Thresholding a smooth random map gives connected fields. Fitted sizes and arrangement support further shape tests, but the text explicitly separates largely random inputs as a proposed source from direct connectivity measurements. Mainali pp. 1110–1118 support that distinction.

questions.question: Does “explains the variety” turn statistical agreement into proof of a circuit?
questions.answer: The following limits rule this out: examined statistics are described, connections are unmeasured, and a combined circuit is left open.

unresolved: Memory/place flow reviews must confirm all-chapter main-text and prerequisite promises.

questions.question: Are the reader paths and optional-note promise supported?
questions.answer: The inspected eye path follows calibration, shared variance, timing and circuit explanation. The inverse-filter folds contain additional coefficient and gain derivations while the main text supplies the relation, response and interpretation. The all-chapter promise requires the other groups’ flow checks.

questions.question: Can a local review establish that every needed explanation stays in the main text?
questions.answer: Only on the inspected eye path and its checked prerequisites. The coordinator agreed to reconcile the whole-book promise with the memory and place reviewers.

questions.question: Does the model/derivation distinction retain biological assumptions?
questions.answer: Yes. A spike disturbance supplies the neural setting before projection and probability. An ideal estimator is separated from biological implementation. Appendix I–VII and page starts 1,3,6,9,10,12,17 match the original contents.

questions.question: Does the appendix map imply that algebra demonstrates neural implementation?
questions.answer: The text explicitly requires separate evidence that the animal implements the computation and retains assumptions on both reading paths.

questions.question: Does the diffusion convention match the eye calculations?
questions.answer: Yes. D sets spreading and M=2Dt is restricted to an unbiased unbounded one-dimensional model with constant D. The timing chapter uses this convention before deriving the filtered output. Constructed checks are separated from reproduction of empirical work.

questions.question: Could 2Dt be read as the measured-eye law despite filtering?
questions.answer: The text labels it the basic model; the eye introduction requires a mapping through muscles and the timing chapter derives the changed law.

questions.question: Do source identities and supporting-file descriptions match?
questions.answer: Titles, authors, years and DOIs agree with the local published sources. The 2012 main PDF has Early Edition pages 1–6 and its appendix contents reach page 20. Mainali has a cover before the article.

questions.question: Does an apparent equation inconsistency claim author-confirmed correction?
questions.answer: No. The closing sentence explicitly identifies independent mathematical checks, not author-confirmed corrections.

questions.question: What is observed and what is proposed?
questions.answer: Recorded OMN activity supports shared upstream drive; a wandering stored position is proposed by the model. Calibration puts the prediction on the displacement scale needed for the later common-variance ratio.

questions.question: Does “same scale” incorrectly make matching units necessary for every correlation?
questions.answer: In context “this comparison” concerns neural diffusion, eye trajectory and calibrated shared contribution. The later rate analysis separately compares rate predictions.

questions.question: What acts on what?
questions.answer: The integrator maintains the position command, OMNs activate muscles, and the ocular plant produces movement. Common input, private generated spike noise and downstream or measurement variability are distinguished. Main pp. 5–7 and Methods support these roles.

questions.question: Does a common command surviving averaging imply every shared input survives any neuron-sign combination?
questions.answer: No. This is the calibrated position command of the relevant population. Later motor equations show its unit gain; private fluctuations are said only to partly cancel.

questions.question: Which independence can these recordings test directly?
questions.answer: They record one OMN paired with eye motion, not simultaneous OMN pairs. The published peer response confirms this. Main Methods supports two male macaques, 25 kHz/1 kHz sampling, 30 ms exclusions and 350 ms segmentation.

questions.question: Do 57 cells supply 57 independent animal samples or establish intrinsic-noise independence?
questions.answer: The text expressly rejects both inferences and states gain transfer as an assumption.

questions.question: Are the forward fit, units and evaluation correct?
questions.answer: Firing at t predicts movement at t plus the neural lead. Coefficients multiply angle, velocity and acceleration to spikes/s. Eqs. 2–3 and Methods support interval-derived rate, loss, 21 ms smoothing, 20 Hz exclusion and held-out-trial predictions.

questions.question: Does m measure eye mass, or does the p value give the common-variance fraction?
questions.answer: Both readings are excluded: m is a fitted combined coefficient, and the rate correlation is explicitly before any common-share estimate.

questions.question: Does inversion preserve gain, delay and units?
questions.answer: Factoring mp²+rp+k gives the stated decay times. The impulse conditions h(0+)=0 and m h′(0+)=1 fix the coefficient. Kernel area is 1/k and positive neural lead delays the response. Values recompute to 2.173913, area 0.25 and a 20 degree offset at 80 spikes/s.

questions.question: Would unit-area normalization or reversing the delay preserve the common fraction?
questions.answer: No. The retained 1/k and delayed response match main Eqs. 4–7. The equal-decay limit is u exp(-u/tau)/m.

questions.question: Why can weak correlations reject independent motor noise alone?
questions.answer: Least-squares explained fraction is R². For standardized uncorrelated predictors residual variance is 1 minus sum Ri², so average Ri² is at most 1/Nm. Mean R² is at least mean R squared. 0.17²=0.0289 exceeds 1/1000=0.001.

questions.question: Is R² the goodness of the raw predictor, or does this prove anatomical independence?
questions.answer: No. It is the fitted-gain explained fraction. Representative sampling and the separate biological independence premise are explicit, matching Supplementary S1–S2 and Discussion.

questions.question: Why is chi distinct from R² and what is its error?
questions.answer: Unit common gain and uncorrelated components give Cov(X,Y)=Var(C). Chi divides by movement variance; R by both standard deviations. The example gives R=0.1700016 and chi=0.82. Inverse-variance weighting minimizes independent estimation variance and gives the stated propagated error.

questions.question: Do out-of-range sample estimates invalidate the true fraction or turn 0.82 into a one-cell prediction score?
questions.answer: No. Estimator versus fraction is distinguished. Main Eqs. 11–17 and Fig. 2 support the result; the constructed case has R²=2.89 percent while chi=82 percent.

questions.question: What remains open after a one-lag common-share estimate?
questions.answer: It cannot distinguish fluctuations around a stable value from accumulated changes. The opening proposes lag-dependent MSD after checking measurement error.

questions.question: Does a common fraction already establish Brownian dynamics?
questions.answer: No. The opening explicitly leaves that question open and motivates the lag-dependent comparison.

questions.question: Why is the correction twice the single-position error variance?
questions.answer: A positive-lag difference contains two independent errors; variances add and mixed movement/error terms vanish. At zero lag the identical error cancels. 0.0014-0.0010=0.0004 and 0.0001 is 25 percent. Main 18–19, ED2 and the peer response support the procedure.

questions.question: Does a short-lag plateau imply nonzero zero-lag MSD or justify smoothing the trajectory?
questions.answer: No. The zero-lag exception and the distortion caused by smoothing are explicit. This corrects an average statistic, not individual unknown noise.

questions.question: Do the two filtered inputs produce the claimed MSDs?
questions.answer: White-input covariance is a shifted kernel overlap, yielding a plateau for a stable decaying kernel. Brownian-command velocity has Cv(s)=D exp(-|s|/tau)/tau, giving MSD 2D[lag-tau(1-exp(-lag/tau))]. The short/long slopes are 2 and 1; values at tau and 5tau recompute to 1.718282 and 1.239490.

questions.question: Does this differentiate a Brownian path ordinarily, or exclude all correlated peripheral inputs?
questions.answer: Neither. The stochastic integral is taught as weighted independent increments; velocity belongs to the filtered output. The final paragraph preserves slow correlated peripheral sources.

questions.question: Does the circuit follow uniquely from the recordings and MSD?
questions.answer: No. Neither result identifies the circuit. The proposed model must generate eye motion through OMNs and muscles and match both magnitude and timing.

questions.question: Does curve agreement prove the integrator was recorded or selectively tested?
questions.answer: The opening denies unique localization and the limits section names both missing tests.

questions.question: Do the equations explain persistence and the full signal path?
questions.answer: Saturated spike inputs drive synaptic states; their weighted difference is EOI. With F=0, summing gives tau_s dEOI/dt=-EOI+G(EOI); G(z)=z gives a fixed continuum and G′=1 local neutrality. Active motor units transmit EOI at steady state. Main 23–34 and parameters match.

questions.question: Is common gain valid below threshold, or does 70 ms forbid short-lag feedback effects?
questions.answer: The gain argument is limited to active units. The feedback paragraph distinguishes lag from time after a perturbation, includes immediate -A EOI, and matches ED3 amplitude effects across lags.

questions.question: Are absolute slope, fractional slope and regularity kept distinct?
questions.answer: Every Mth Poisson spike gives CV=1/sqrt(M) at constant rate. Renewal counts give lambda L CV². J=Na²/lambda0 yields the fixed-geometry scale CV² lambda0/(N a² tau_s²). Substituting b=a/lambda0 gives the inverse-rate form. The drift CV is 0.0024056; 2D=100 arcmin²/s is 0.0277778 deg²/s.

questions.question: Can inverse-rate scaling use absolute slope, or can low interval CV alone imply low count variance for all processes?
questions.answer: No. The units objection to printed Eq. 1 is labeled a guide interpretation; slope definitions and renewal/constant-rate conditions are explicit.

questions.question: Do figures have the correct evidential roles?
questions.answer: The table separates rate correlation, common variance, private-noise mismatch, simulated internal diffusion and full-model/method tests. Main captions support all five. Supplement captions support -0.09±0.22 and retained internal stochastic spikes in ED10.

questions.question: Does the output-noise control remove internal diffusion noise, or is the Figure 4 valley a measured brain energy function?
questions.answer: The text says internal stochastic spikes remain; the table calls the valley a schematic. Both agree with original captions.

questions.question: What causal conclusion remains unproved?
questions.answer: The data support shared upstream drive and the model can reproduce motion, but integrator neurons were not recorded or selectively perturbed. Noisy input or already diffusive upstream signals remain possible, as Discussion and the published peer response state.

questions.question: Does matching amplitude/slope uniquely establish the necessary circuit or recover its parameters?
questions.answer: No. Both claims are explicitly excluded, with missing tests and alternative sources named.

questions.question: Does Part II state the next questions accurately?
questions.answer: It separates the command-to-muscle eye path, spatial firing/model comparisons and a synthesis of untested connections. This matches the eye path and the primary spatial paper.

questions.question: Does the title imply all studies establish one complete neural code?
questions.answer: No. It says different parts, and the purpose lists distinct questions and untested connections.
